title: DST Placement Coordination
name: DST Placement Coordination
metaTitle: DST Placement Coordination in San Diego, CA
metaDescription: DST placement coordination for San Diego exchanges when direct replacement property is too thin, with fee loads and liquidity terms read line by line.

sections.html: A Delaware statutory trust gives a San Diego investor a way to complete an exchange with fractional, passive ownership in institutional-grade property when the direct replacement market is too thin or too fast-moving to close on time. It is a fallback for a specific situation, not a shortcut, and the offering documents behind it need the same scrutiny as any other identified property.

sections.heading: What the Glossy Summary Sheet Does Not Show
sections.html: Every DST sponsor produces a clean one-page summary with a projected yield and a photo of the building. What that sheet rarely spells out clearly is the layered fee structure, acquisition fees, asset management fees, and a sponsor promote on the back end, that sits between the property's actual performance and what an investor eventually receives. Reading the summary sheet alone is how people end up surprised at the net return.

sections.heading: The Liquidity Terms That Get Buried in the Offering Memo
sections.html: A DST interest is illiquid for the life of the hold, typically five to ten years, with no secondary market to speak of if an investor's circumstances change. The offering memorandum will disclose this, but usually many pages after the projected returns, not next to them. For San Diego investors weighing a DST against a direct replacement in Torrey Pines-adjacent life science or coastal multifamily, that liquidity gap is often the deciding factor once it is actually understood.

sections.heading: Why San Diego Investors End Up Looking at DSTs at All
sections.html: Tight inventory across San Diego's industrial, office-lab, and coastal multifamily submarkets means an investor can reach day 40 of the identification window with no direct replacement that pencils. A DST placed on the identification letter alongside direct candidates gives a real fallback that can close quickly, since the trust structure is designed for exchange timelines. It should not be the only name on the letter unless direct options have genuinely been exhausted.

sections.heading: What Gets Reviewed Before a DST Goes on the Letter
sections.html:
Before recommending a DST as part of an identification strategy, we work through:

  • Full fee schedule across acquisition, management, and disposition
  • Sponsor track record and prior full-cycle performance, where available
  • Debt structure and whether it is recourse to the trust or the investor
  • Property-level details behind the projected yield, beyond the headline number

sections.heading: Coordination, Not a Securities Recommendation
sections.html: DST interests are securities, and any placement has to go through a licensed broker-dealer or registered representative, not through us. Our role is coordinating the timeline and comparing the offering terms against your exchange requirements. Confirm suitability, fees, and risk with a licensed securities professional and your tax advisor before committing capital.

sections.heading: Comparing Two DST Offerings Side by Side
sections.html:
Two DST offerings with similar projected yields can carry very different real economics once the full fee load and debt structure are laid out next to each other. One sponsor's acquisition fee might be absorbed into the purchase price rather than charged separately, while another discloses it as a distinct line item, making the second one look more expensive even if the total cost to the investor is the same or lower.

We build a side-by-side comparison of every fee, the debt terms, and the sponsor's stated hold period before an investor chooses between DST candidates, since a summary sheet alone rarely makes an apples-to-apples comparison possible on its own.

That comparison also has to account for how each sponsor handles a mid-hold capital call or a shortfall in projected distributions, terms that are disclosed in the offering memorandum but rarely discussed until an investor asks directly. Two DSTs with identical projected yields on paper can carry very different exposure once that fine print is actually compared side by side.

We ask each sponsor directly how a shortfall in distributions has been handled historically on other offerings, since a sponsor's actual track record through a soft patch tells you more than a projected number ever will.

Sponsors with a longer operating history are usually more forthcoming about a past shortfall than one marketing its first offering, simply because there is a record to point to either way. That history is worth requesting directly rather than assuming a clean projection reflects how every prior deal actually performed.

A sponsor unwilling to share that record on request is telling you something about how a rough patch on this specific offering might eventually be communicated to investors.

faqs.q: When does a DST make sense for a San Diego exchange?
faqs.a: Usually when direct replacement property in the target submarket is too thin or moving too fast to close within the exchange deadline, and a passive, fractional structure fits the investor's goals.
They are disclosed in the offering memorandum, but often many pages past the projected return summary. Ask for the full fee schedule directly rather than relying on the one-page overview.

faqs.q: Can I sell my DST interest early if I need the cash?
faqs.a: Generally no. DST interests are illiquid for the life of the hold, typically five to ten years, with limited to no secondary market.

faqs.q: Who can actually sell me a DST interest?
faqs.a: A licensed broker-dealer or registered representative, since DST interests are securities. We coordinate the exchange timeline and terms comparison, not the sale itself.

faqs.q: Should a DST be my only identified property?
faqs.a: Not by default. A DST works well as a backup alongside direct candidates, especially in a market as supply-constrained as San Diego, but relying on it exclusively removes flexibility if terms change before closing.
